Long-term demand visibility matters more than shareholder returns
Prices continue rising as shipments ramp up
We maintain our target price of W3,100,000 for SK Hynix. The stock remains undervalued in absolute terms, trading at a 2027F P/E of 2.7x and 2027F P/B of 1.4x. Notably, our target price implies multiples of just 5.7x and 3.0x, respectively. We raised our operating profit forecasts for 4Q26 and 2027 by 15% and 14% to W108tr (+30% QoQ) and W489tr (+69% YoY), respectively.
In 3Q26, DRAM bit shipments rose 9.7% QoQ, supported by increased sales of HBM4 and server DDR5, while NAND bit shipments edged down 0.8% QoQ as sales focused primarily on 321-layer enterprise SSDs. ASP growth was in the high-20% range for DRAM and the mid-20% range for NAND. In 4Q26, we expect DRAM bit shipment growth (QoQ) to reach the mid-20% range, driven by the expansion of the 1c process and the ramp-up of M15X.
Long-term demand visibility matters more than shareholder returns
SK Hynix announced plans to return approximately W100tr to shareholders in 2026, including at least W60tr in share buybacks and cancellations and at least W30tr in cash dividends. The company also plans to conduct share buybacks every quarter under its policy to return at least 50% of free cash flow to shareholders. More significant than the expanded shareholder returns, however, was management’s confidence in the sustainability of demand through 2029.
For 2027, management projected demand growth (adjusted for supply constraints) in the mid-20% range for DRAM and the high teens for NAND, similar to this year’s levels. With AI infrastructure investment broadening beyond big tech companies to other enterprises and governments, the company expects memory shortages to persist through 2030 due to the increasing complexity of advanced manufacturing processes, the time required for new fab build-outs, and extended production lead times.
SK Hynix has signed long-term agreements, typically covering five years, with 14 major customers, including leading cloud service providers. These agreements cover more than 50% of total production capacity for 2027?28. Including volumes under negotiation, DRAM and HBM capacity through 2029 is effectively fully booked. Pricing will reflect market conditions within agreed ranges, while deposits and other safeguard measures should provide downside protection for earnings.
Customer demand for HBM exceeds available supply by more than twofold. With negotiations on 2027 HBM volumes and pricing nearing completion, we expect HBM margins to gradually rise toward those of conventional DRAM. Improving HBM margins should strengthen the incentive to expand production. Given HBM’s higher wafer capacity requirements per bit, this expansion should displace a disproportionate amount of conventional DRAM capacity, keeping DRAM supply tight.
